comment_content:
before taking this course, you need to ask yourself: do you have the prerequisites?
roughly in the order of importance:
- some level of mandarin AND cantonese (spoken): if you aren't proficient in both, you'll struggle a lot in the phonology section, because the questions are roughly split half and half between mandarin and cantonese. if you only know mandarin, go take huma 1060. if you only know cantonese, go take huma 2031.
- good sense of "白話文" structure: this one's for the morphology and syntax parts. good luck if you're just bad at chinese like me, because you'll fall behind there no matter how hard you study.
- ipa: everything's in ipa, so you'll need to learn it, but if you've already learned it, you'll be way ahead of everyone else in phonology. you don't need to know all the symbols by heart, but you should know how to use the ipa in general, not just in english. knowing english ipa is helpful though, because there are somehow questions asking that even though it's "structure of chinese"...
- jyutping and pinyin: both of them translate pretty well into his system. it's not ipa, but it does mean that you only need to learn the symbols themselves, not how to transcribe your speech.
if you wanna do well in this course (think A/A+), definitely study ipa between semesters.
actual course outline:
1. introduction
2. chinese phonology: speech sounds and tones, romanization systems (never tested?), syllable structure
3. chinese morphology: morpheme and word, word formation process
4. chinese syntax: word classes, word order, sentence structure
5. topics in language situation and dialects across china: linguistic neighbors of the chinese language, defining language and dialect, major chinese dialects
6. brief evolution of different dialects
7. basic knowledge about chinese writing system

comment_content:
Basically a history of Western classical music course, going from ancient/Medieval music all the way to the Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic and 20th century.
You learn what music sounded like in each period and why it changed, together with some historical events, cultural ideas, famous composers and their more important pieces.
No music background is really needed. There are music terms and theory to remember, but nothing super technical like actually composing or playing music.
There are quite a lot of forms and terms to know, like sonata form, rondo, fugue, opera seria/buffa, leitmotif, Impressionism, Expressionism etc. You also need to know roughly when they appeared and which composers/styles they are related to.
There is a listening part in the tests, where they play part of one of the pieces covered in class and you have to recognise the piece/composer. Definitely listen to the playlist a few times beforehand because some pieces become really easy to recognise once you've heard them enough.
For the normal test questions, it's mostly stuff from the lecture slides: history, composers, definitions, musical forms and characteristics of different periods. There are quite a lot of little details, but it's not too bad if you revise the slides properly.
The professor also plays quite a lot of music and opera during class, so it's not just sitting there reading music history for the whole lecture.
Overall probably my favourite course this semester. Pretty chill and genuinely interesting, especially compared with more technical courses. I didn't expect to enjoy classical music history that much, but by the end I could actually recognise different styles and understand why the music sounds the way it does.

comment_workload:
[Warning: A Bit Long]
TERRIBLE and HORRIBLE. That’s my final answer for answering the topic of this post. 
According to USTSPACE, MATH 1014 is rated as having a workload of C. If that rating is accurate, then the workload of this course deserves an F—or even a G—assuming C truly reflects the workload of MATH 1014.
I genuinely believe the professor does not respect students. The assessments consist of:
1) Weekly Assignments  
A student posted one of the weekly assignments on USTSPACE—please refer to their comment. Based on my experience, each assignment takes 6–7 hours per week (if you skim ALL the materials and use GenAI slightly). Without GenAI, it can take more than 10 hours. Yet each assignment is worth only 2%.  
Reading materials are posted just a few days (around 3) before the deadline.  
-Marks are graded in increments of 0.1, meaning every decimal can affect your final grade.
2) Book Reviews ×2  
You must read the books thoroughly to write something meaningful, which takes another 6–7 hours. These often overlap with weekly assignments.  
- Graded with 0.1 mark precision (e.g., 11.2/15), but feedback is vague—just “Great job!” or “Nice work!”  
The grading criteria are unclear—possibly based on subjective impressions.
3–5) Final Deliverables During Exam Week  
- Rough Cut and Timeline
- Video
- Paper
Although the course claims to have no final exam, many students enroll expecting a lighter workload. Ironically, the instructor scheduled a film competition during the exam period, worth 1 mark.
- You must attend for 3 hours during exam week to earn it.  
- Assignments 3–5 are also due during the examination period.
Actually, all of the above is just a piece of cake, as it’s written in the syllabus and the instructor kept reminding us during the add/drop period. So if you chose to stay in the course, you should accept it.
What’s truly terrible is that the professor keeps adding “extra bonus marks” activities and assignments.
“Bonus” Marks That Aren’t Really Bonus  
These were not listed in the syllabus, but became essential for anyone aiming for an A-range grade:
6) Two extra weekly assignments (Syllabus said 10, ended up with 12) → 4 bonus marks
7) Three talks with written feedback → 3 bonus marks  
8) In-class questions (0.5 marks each, but students rarely answered, I guess you can ignore it)  
9) Film competition attendance → 1 mark  
Total “Bonus” Marks: At least 8 marks, added without prior notice.  
One talk was announced via email on the same morning it was held. If you want an A-range grade, these “bonuses” are not optional—they’re compulsory.
Personal Reflections
1) The Darkest Day
When I received the Canvas notification titled *“The First Book Review and Weekly Assignment”*, I cried near Canteen II. I even considered ending my life. That’s a true story—I was overwhelmed with quizzes and felt hopeless. I’m deeply thankful to my friends who supported me. That was my darkest day at HKUST.
2) The Film Competition
During exam week, I attended the film session. When the professor announced that attendees would receive 1 bonus mark, the class cheered. I couldn’t. I felt like a poor soul following the professor’s unreasonable demands. I couldn’t feel happy.  
I don’t understand why HKUST students (myself included) are so marks-oriented. One girl spoke up during (other official) class to challenge the professor—but no one supported her. We all stayed silent, myself included.
I really agree with the comment of teaching in one of the posts of HUMA 1430 -  "Unable to understand students' concerns worries or questions."
Final Advice  
Believe me—you’ll regret enrolling in this course. The fast-moving waitlist was a warning. The course enrollment system is a market. Trust the market mechanism. Save your time. Don’t enroll.

comment_content:
Haha, I survived this so-called "bad grade" course. 
To be honest, as a fan of modern Chinese history, it wasn't that hard for those who did previous research on it.
The course covered the history of China from early Qing to the reform & open-up in the PRC era. Besides historical facts, Prof Cheung did a great job of inspiring students to think beyond those written facts by historians. Knowing "WHY" and "HOW" China came to today is an important gateway for your China Studies.
More importantly, for new year 1 GCS students, this is a crucial opportunity to develop the necessary essay writing and information processing proficiency. Through the course assignment, you will learn how to modify your essay framework, identify the key factors, and more.
I was not a history student back in my high school time, but I got a pretty good grade at last. Therefore, don't worry too much about the course! As long as you make your effort (and more personal research), you should be able to get a good grade

Warning: *THIS IS A HUMA COURSE, ITS HUMA1710 NOT MATH1710.*
Only 6 modules, over a whole semester. The course significantly references a book by 李天命. The first module is useless for quizzes. 
The content ideas could be interesting, but course designs skims over the surface and fails to connect underlying dots and drains intricacy, leaving only surface values precipitating as boring memorization of specific examples and special cases, rather than built on solid theoretical foundations and rigor.
If you want to sign up for the course for enrichment of the soul, you might wanna think again. This is a game of "Simon says" (calling it Lewis says is more appropriate) HUMA course disguised as a rigorous study of logic and linguistic elements. Judging from other reviews, you *might be tempted into believing* the course is about juggling with logic operators, and formalising statements and pinpointing fallacies using rules of syllogism and inference. In reality, you are dealing with scattered, unfocused and frail-structured materials littered everywhere, most of these cannot be derived from first principles. 
Not to mention the lecture notes are practically useless (they are only an inch long and does not contain materials relevant to exams at all) and it is by intentional design that you must spend dozens of hours going through every second of the lecture videos trying to find hints (if any) which Lewis drops seemingly at random to "reward those who listen to his lectures". Mind you it is not possible to know the solutions to a good number of the quiz problems without the hints. 
Directly reading the book by 李天命 is a substantially more fulfilling experience.

-understand the interrelationship between music, literature, drama and culture 
-understand the elements of exoticism in western opera 
-analyze the structure of scenes 
-critique production quality 
-coordinate team activities 
-give and take direction and constructive criticism \ communicate orally applicable to presentation 
-express their own talent and creativity 
Essentially put, teaching you how to 赏析 (Appreciate and Analyze) Western Opera works, introducing knowledge surrounding the art types, some (a lot of) proper nouns (in Italian), overall, if you have background in classical music and some interest in theatre productions, you would be able to find this class interesting, given the instructor's enthusiasm.
Other side content includes periods and musical philosophies at the time, and by extension, the evolution of opera styles. Composers' lives and some fun facts (e.g. how Mozart composed Don Giovanni the hour before its premiere).
